aic:75574.texto: Ching Tsai Loo (C.T. Loo, 1880‒1957), Paris and New York; sold to the Art Institute of Chicago, Oct. 10, 1951.
aic:75574.title: Song of a Fisherman

aic:75574.texto:
Wang Wen exemplified the life of the scholar-official in Ming dynasty China. He retired from government service to his lakeside retreat and pursued painting, calligraphy, and poetry. For this painting, Wang Wen wrote a poem (also entitled “Song of a Fisherman”), which includes several allusions to moral integrity. This poem displays the artist’s distinctively fluid, cursive “draft script” (cao shu). Its first section reads as follows:
Most men of the world fish with crooked hooks: I alone trust in hooks, but never in fancy baits. After rain, I carry my long pole to the terrace edge and dangle if from among pines and clouds above the ripples of Qi. (translated by Irving Yucheng Lo)
Qi refers to a river in north-central China. This river is cited in several verses of the Shijing (Book of Odes) – a compilation of more than three hundred poems datable between about 1000 and 600 B.C that extol men of principle. Government officials often alluded to these poems to convey Confucian teachings.
aic:75574.title: Song of a Fisherman

cma:147045.title: Solitary Colors of the Autumn Woods

cma:147045.texto: Two gentlemen stand outside a thatched hut in a dense forest; some trees have bare branches indicating that the season is early autumn. Wang Jianzhang’s inscribed poem refers to a chapter called “Autumn Water” from Zhuangzi, a famous Daoist text written in the 3rd century BC: "Cold frost falls on the fences, / Solitary colors scatter the maples. / Reciting the chapter of “The Autumn Water,” / I cannot still the emotion in my old heart." Wang Jianzhang lived through the collapse of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) and the rise of the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), when China was governed by the Manchus, an ethnic people from Manchuria who were traditionally viewed as “barbarians” by the Chinese. The poetic reference to Zhuangzi’s “Autumn Water” seems to discreetly convey Wang’s feelings about his country being taken over. “Autumn Water” was about learning to take steps in the foreign way, but not acquiring a foreign tongue. Perhaps Wang was lamenting his conflicted situation. For survival he had to adapt to the new political and social climate, while still trying to maintain his own identity and Chinese traditions.
cma:147045.title: Solitary Colors of the Autumn Woods

cma:148359.texto:
(Sotheby Parke Bernet, Inc., New York, NY)
The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, OH
cma:148359.title: Bamboo in Wind

cma:148359.texto:
East Asian paintings from China, Korea, and Japan were frequently conceived as sets of multiple images. These sets might have been composed for specific palace or temple rooms, or to portray a specific theme, such as the four seasons. Over time, the original intent of such sets is often lost through damage, changes in ownership, or a variety of other reasons. 

The identity of the artist can also be lost, but then, sometimes, retrieved. This pair of ink paintings has traditionally been labeled as Japanese and attributed to the 16th-century painter Genga. Since there are no seals or signature of the artist on the painting, this attribution was based on comparisons of brush style with paintings known to be by Genga. More recent study indicates that while the 16th century is an appropriate time frame for the pair, the precise cultural identity of the artist is not certain after all. The dark, eccentric shapes of the rocks and bamboo clusters and the dramatic tonal contrasts evident throughout the composition point to either Korean authorship or influence upon a Japanese painter of the period.
cma:148359.title: Bamboo in Wind

cma:151223.texto: Born in Okayama in western Japan, samurai Fujimoto Tesseki learned literati painting before abandoning his local government position to travel the country studying calligraphy, military science, painting, and poetry. He funded his training with sales of his calligraphies and paintings and later founded a school of Japanese studies and martial arts near Kyoto. Despite his skill with ink, Tesseki may be better remembered for his politics. Opposed to the military government of his era, he wanted a return to direct rule by the emperor, a cause for which he died in battle.
cma:151223.title: Autumn in a Mountain Valley

cma:152826.texto: Lu Tong (d. 835) was a Tang dynasty poet and tea aficionado.
cma:152826.title: Lu Tong and Servant

cma:152826.texto: Min Zhen, who was orphaned at age 12 and developed an eccentric personality, was trained by Tang Yin (1682–1756), a writer, playwright, and superintendent of the imperial porcelain workshops in Jingdezhen. The connection to him may have enabled Min to stay in Beijing for a decade from around 1773. It is not clear whether he ever resided in Yangzhou, but his style is in many instances reminiscent of that of Yangzhou artist Huang Shen. This album demonstrates Min’s versatility and mature style in the last years of his life.
cma:152826.title: Lu Tong and Servant

latencia.nota: 🔑 **Esto acota el recuadro ⚠️ de la observabilidad.** Ahí se declaraba que *las etapas puras no tienen span* —el `Fusionador` y el `RenderizadorDeSalida` no llaman a ningún puerto— y que por lo tanto *prometer latencia por etapa sobre-promete*. Instrumentando en el **`EjecutorDeEtapas`**, que es el lugar que ese mismo recuadro señala, **sí hay latencia para las ocho**. la latencia por etapa deja de estar sobre-prometido. **Va reportado.**

nota_de_identidad: Clase 2 (la tabla de identidades): *registro de una ejecución*. La identidad fija **las entradas, no la salida** —una salida no determinista con la misma entrada es el dato que el muestreo fijado, registrado y con su variabilidad medida mide—, así que lleva **ordinal** y la regla de que un id determina su contenido no aplica. El ordinal se **reserva** creando el directorio de forma exclusiva: `1 + n` es un *leer, después escribir* y el barrido es paralelo.
nota_de_la_tabla: degradación/la regla de qué corridas agregan a la tabla: una corrida con degradación **no planificada** no agrega a la tabla C0–C4 —*una C4 que degradó en silencio entraría etiquetada como C4 comportándose como C3*— y una con degradación **planificada** tampoco: es el criterio de respuesta garantizada y se reporta aparte. Una etapa **ausente por configuración** no degrada: no corre, y por eso C0–C3 sí agregan.
nota_de_ob2: *Los tokens se **persisten en el artefacto de corrida**, no solo en LangSmith* (los tokens en el artefacto de corrida): si el servicio se cae, se pierde la herramienta de debugging, **no los números** que la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo publican. Y el árbol declara qué se trazó y qué no, que es el registro de decisiones hecho artefacto.
